function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that will give you a Docker‑based build, a Kubernetes deployment/service, and a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds & pushes the image whenever you push to `main`.  
All of the files are meant to live in the root of the repository (except the workflow, which goes under `.github/workflows/`).

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) is a very small Node.js “Hello‑World” app.  
> The Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and workflow below are written with that minimal structure in mind (i.e. `app.js` listening on port 3000).  
> If your actual app uses a different entry point, port, or package manager, tweak the values accordingly.

---

## 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Create/Update the following files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:14-alpine

# Metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm install --production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why `node:14-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small (~50 MB) and work well for simple Node.js apps.  
> If you need a newer Node version, change the `FROM` line to `node:16-alpine`, `node:18-alpine`, etc.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image repo
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the Docker Hub (or GHCR) repo you’ll push to.  
> * `replicas:` – number of pods you want running.  
> * `service.type:` – `ClusterIP` is fine for internal traffic; switch to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or GHCR)
      - name: Login to DockerHub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image and push it to the registry
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- same as in k8s.yaml

      # Optional: run tests (uncomment if you have a test script)
      # - name: Run tests
      #   run: npm test
```

> **Secrets you need to add in the GitHub repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (recommended over password)

---

## 3. Add the new/updated files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you already had a Dockerfile or Kubernetes YAML, you can simply overwrite them; `git add` will stage the changes.

---

## 4. Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to Docker Hub.  
You can then deploy to Kubernetes with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

---

### Quick sanity checks

| Check | Command | Expected Result |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| Docker image built locally | `docker build -t yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest .` | Image appears in `docker images` |
| Docker image runs | `docker run -p 3000:3000 yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest` | Visiting `http://localhost:3000` shows your app |
| Kubernetes deployment | `kubectl get deployments` | `nodejs-welcome` shows 2 replicas |
| Kubernetes service | `kubectl get svc` | `nodejs-welcome` shows port 3000 |

---

## Recap of the files

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── Dockerfile
├── k8s.yaml
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── ci.yml
└── (existing app files: app.js, package.json, etc.)
```

That’s it! After pushing, your repo will automatically build & publish a Docker image on every commit to `main`, and you’ll have a ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes manifest. Happy coding!
